2.1: `kubectl run` can generate the pod for you, including the port and the labels, so start from a dry-run YAML and create the namespace first.
The generated container is named after the pod (`webpod`), so rename it to `webcont` in the YAML; `--port` becomes `containerPort` and `--labels` takes a comma-separated list.
2.2: Create the Service with a generator or plain YAML rather than exposing the pod, because you want control over exactly which labels the Service selects.

`kubectl expose` copies all pod labels into the selector, while `create service clusterip` defaults the selector to `app: <name>`; edit it to `type: webserver`, and map `port` 8080 to `targetPort` 80.
2.3: You do not need to recreate the Service; modify the existing one with `patch` or `edit`.
Set `spec.type` to NodePort and add `nodePort: 30080` inside the existing `spec.ports[]` entry; if you patch the ports list, repeat the whole entry (`port`, `targetPort`, `protocol`).
2.4: Generate a single-container pod YAML with a dry run, then add a second entry to the containers list by hand.
Rename the generated container to `web`, and give `logger` a `command` array of `sh`, `-c`, and the loop string so the busybox container keeps running (otherwise it exits and READY is not 2/2).
2.5: A native sidecar is an init container that keeps running alongside the main containers, and both containers share an `emptyDir` volume.
Put `restartPolicy: Always` on the entry under `initContainers` to make it a sidecar, and mount the `logs` volume at `/var/log/app` in both containers; mind the escaped quotes in the app command.
2.6: A Deployment can be created fully from the command line, and its ReplicaSet carries the Deployment's `app` label.
`kubectl create deployment` accepts `--replicas` and `--port`; `-o name` would add a `replicaset.apps/` prefix, so select the ReplicaSet by label and print only `.metadata.name` with jsonpath.
2.7: The Deployment controller reconciles the desired state, so deleting its ReplicaSet or a pod is only temporary; select the ReplicaSet by label rather than by its generated name.
Use `delete rs -l app=firstdeploy`, and for the pod use `$(...)` with `get po -o name` to pick one; then check READY on the Deployment returns to 3/3.
2.8: Pods are mostly immutable, but a few fields can change in place, and there is a dedicated kubectl subcommand for changing images.
`kubectl set image` takes `pod/<name>` and then `<container-name>=<new-image>`, so use the container name `webcont`; the kubelet restarts that container, which is why RESTARTS becomes 1.
2.9: Use `kubectl api-resources` for short names, API groups and the namespaced flag, and `kubectl explain` with the dotted field path for types.

In the `api-resources` output the short name is the SHORTNAMES column, the group/version is the APIVERSION column, and NAMESPACED is true/false; `explain` shows the field type for `runAsUser`, which is an integer.
2.10: Describe the pod and read the Events at the bottom to find the first failure, then check what happens after you fix it, since there is more than one problem.

One problem is the image tag typo; the other is the `command` running nginx with `daemon on;`, which backgrounds the process so PID 1 exits. Remove the `command` (or use `daemon off;`), and delete the old pod before re-applying since pod specs are largely immutable.
2.11: Query pods across all namespaces and format the output so only the names remain, then filter by prefix.
Use `-A` with `--no-headers` and `-o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name`, then `grep '^coredns'` anchored at the start of the name.
